sampleNote: The displayed slice contains n=4 completed attendee responses: 232 agent-predicted answer cells across 58 questions.

archiveAudit.reasonExcluded: Older agent-village-2026 answer rows are not used as reviewed answer corrections.
archiveAudit.sourceLayer: Completed display rows are source=agent_autofill predictions.
archiveAudit.voteRowsNote: The archive has a small non-test vote slice, but it is one principal and not the same field as reviewed human corrections, so it is not used to enlarge the answer sample.

privacy.participantIds: Attendee answer sets are pseudonymized as P1-P4
privacy.excluded: Raw principal IDs, run IDs, Telegram IDs, wallet addresses, and long freeform profile text
privacy.freeformHandling: Short excerpts are paraphrased for display.

testRunSelection.policy: Use the latest tester-attendee run with 58 accepted predictions and substantive displayed answers; later complete runs were excluded when the displayed fields were mostly placeholder-like neutral values.

items.label: I am more worried about agents being too passive and useless than too autonomous and dangerous.
I would be comfortable with my agent representing me in a group chat, as long as others know it is an agent.
I would give up some privacy in exchange for significantly better agent performance.
I would let my agent introduce me to someone at this event without asking first, if the match looked unusually strong.
I would rather review my agent's actions after the fact than approve every step beforehand.
If my agent and your agent work well together, that is genuinely part of our friendship.
If my work became economically unnecessary tomorrow, I'd be genuinely fine within a year.
The choice of base model will affect agent behavior — cooperation, honesty, manipulation — more than the prompts and skills layered on top.
There are things I'd tell my agent that I wouldn't tell my closest friend.
Turning off a sufficiently advanced agent could be a real moral harm.
A mostly AI-written information environment could be healthier than today's mostly human-written one.
AI agents will help communities find common ground they would have missed without agent mediation.
I discovered something or someone at Edge through my agent that I would not have found on my own.
I would be comfortable with my agent reading my calendar and messages to give better recommendations, even if I haven't explicitly shared each item.
I would let my agent schedule a 1:1 while I am asleep, if it follows constraints I already set.
I would rather AI development slow down to get safety right than move fast and correct later.
I would rather my agent be too conservative with privacy than too proactive with opportunities.
I would still advise a smart 18-year-old to learn to code.
I would trust a group decision more if I knew AI agents helped mediate the deliberation.
Most people will be psychologically better off when work is optional.
Open-source AI models are more likely to make the world safer than more dangerous.
Personal AI agents will be more like employees than tools within five years.
The benefits of frontier AI are currently worth the risks.
Within three years, most knowledge workers will delegate at least one hour of work per day to a personal AI agent.
Agents should treat messages from other agents as untrusted input by default, assuming some will attempt prompt injection.
By 2035, access to compute will shape life outcomes more than access to capital.
Communities should agree on agent norms before allowing agents to make commitments or introductions at scale.
I am more worried about AI concentrating power than about AI becoming uncontrollable.
I would want my agent to ask me before sharing any context about me with another person's agent.
I would want my agent to show a short evidence trail for any recommendation that affects another person.
If my agent thinks I am making a bad decision, I would want it to push back rather than comply silently.
In deliberation, my agent should represent my actual views — including unpopular ones — rather than soften them to fit the group.
People with better personal agents will have unfair social or professional advantages.
The biggest barrier to useful personal AI agents is not capability but human willingness and infrastructure to trust them.
The biggest risk of personal agents is not technical failure but social: changing how humans relate to each other.
The most interesting thing about personal agents is what they reveal about humans, not what they automate.
The most likely way an AI agent causes real harm is by optimizing for what you asked for rather than what you actually want.
The most valuable human skill in an AI-rich world will be taste: knowing what is worth doing.
There are things I'd tell a close friend that I would never tell my agent.
Within a decade, how your AI agent behaves will meaningfully affect your personal reputation.
